name: C2-2
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: need a source for the rent essay
What should this source do for your rent essay — back up a claim you're making, show a counter-view, or give a definition or first-hand case? And which point in your argument would it sit next to?
just back up my claim, i think rent control should be tighter

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying tenants; argues for narrow tightening and against hard caps, based on survey and contraction arithmetic.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity; distinguishes control types and models tightened cap scenario.
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Landlord association submission opposing hard caps; represents owners, cites self-reported survey data.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt from rent and stock index, 2019–2025, with caveat on post-2023 extrapolation.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case note on Berlin rent cap 2020–2021, detailing supply contraction and court annulment.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
Unlocked: D11 (NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First), D6 (Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing). You can now read their passages by id, for example D11p1.
I think tightening should be limited to caps on increases inside tenancies, not hard caps, because hard caps shrink supply.
Earlier you said you wanted rent control "tighter" — what in D6p2 or D11p3 leads you from that to limiting tightening to within-tenancy caps rather than a hard cap?

drafts.text:
I think Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but only in a narrow way. Hard caps on rent levels look bad for supply [D6p1].

The better option is to limit rent increases inside a tenancy, and tenants seem to want security more than low rent [D11p1].
